intro: Three trees in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, all on the Tennessee side, and each takes some walking. The largest tulip tree in the park, by one count, stands with its top gone at the end of a three-mile climb to Albright Grove. Three old tulip poplars stand together about two and a half miles up the Ramsey Cascades Trail. In Cades Cove, a sweet gum planted on the day of the Pearl Harbor attack grows on a hillside behind a gravel pull-off. If you know other old trees in the park worth the walk, tell us.
meta_description: Old trees in the Great Smoky Mountains: the giant of Albright Grove, the Ramsey Cascades poplars and Cades Cove's Pearl Harbor Tree, with trail distances.
question_meta: Albright Grove's tulip tree, over 25 feet round, is a 6.5-mile round trip; the Ramsey Cascades poplars stand about 2.5 miles up their trail.
question_answer: Two trails lead to the biggest trees on this list. The Maddron Bald Trail near Cosby climbs about 2.9 miles to the Albright Grove Loop, where a tulip tree a little over 25 feet round, which smokymountains.com calls the largest in the park, stands at the end of a short signed spur; the National Park Service gives 6.5 miles round trip. The Ramsey Cascades Trail in Greenbrier passes three big tulip poplars about two and a half miles up, the largest at least seven feet across.
question_context: Big trees in the Smokies are a walk away, and the walks change. Albright Grove is old forest on the Tennessee side in the Cosby area, and several of its giants have died, including a huge snag and a stump that earlier visitors recorded. The tulip tree still called the king of the grove lost its crown, possibly to lightning, and was measured at 25 feet 3 inches round in 2019, the latest published account of it. The Ramsey Cascades Trail was damaged by floods in 2022 and again in 2024, and the park reopened it full-time in 2024 after a three-year restoration; its three poplars were last described in January 2024. In Cades Cove the story is human. Golman Myers planted a sweet gum in his front yard when news of Pearl Harbor reached the cove in December 1941, and in 2022 the park brought Medal of Honor recipients to see it. None of these trees has a published age except that one. Before you drive out, check the park's alerts for trail and road closures, and if you have stood under any of them lately, tell us how they are.

faq.q: Do you need to pay to see these trees?
faq.a: There is no entrance fee for Great Smoky Mountains National Park, and the trails are free to walk. Any vehicle parked for longer than 15 minutes needs a Park It Forward parking tag, at 5 dollars a day, 15 a week or 40 a year, except on the park's free entrance days.

faq.q: How long is the hike to Albright Grove?
faq.a: The National Park Service gives 6.5 miles (10.5 km) round trip from the Maddron Bald Trailhead at the end of Baxter Road, including the 0.7-mile loop through the grove, with about 1,475 feet of climbing on a moderate to steep, rough trail. Parking at the trailhead is limited.

faq.q: Can you get to the trees without a car?
faq.a: No. There is no public transport to any of the three, and no shuttle to the trailheads. Ramsey Prong Road is partly gravel and the Cades Cove Loop Road is one-way and closed to cars on some mornings in season, so check the park's road status before you go.

trees.name: Albright Grove giant tulip tree

location.address: Albright Grove Loop Trail, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Cocke County, Tennessee (TN side)
location.neighbourhood: Cosby, Great Smoky Mountains National Park

trees.story:
The largest tulip tree in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, as smokymountains.com reckons it, has a trunk a little over 25 feet round, about 7.7 metres, and no top. Appalachian Voices measured the girth at 25 feet 3 inches in 2019 and wrote that the crown had been damaged, possibly by lightning, and that the tree may once have stood about 135 feet tall. What remains is a dead-topped veteran that still carries the title king of Albright Grove.

The grove lies on the Tennessee side of the park, in the Cosby area, and reaching it is a proper hike. From the Maddron Bald Trailhead at the end of Baxter Road, off US 321 about 16 miles east of Gatlinburg, the Maddron Bald Trail climbs about 2.9 miles (4.7 km) to the Albright Grove Loop. The National Park Service gives 6.5 miles (10.5 km) round trip including the loop, with about 1,475 feet of climbing that it calls moderate to steep and rough. The tree stands at the end of a short signed spur where the loop starts to descend.

Sources say some trees in the grove are past 200 years old, but none dates this one. Several of the grove's giants have died, and the latest published account of this tree is from 2019. Check the park's trail alerts before you go, and if you have seen it lately, tell us whether it still stands.

Parking for longer than 15 minutes needs a Park It Forward tag.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, a little over 25 feet round, and its dead top. It stands at the end of the short signed spur off the Albright Grove Loop, where the loop starts to descend.
trees.access: From the Maddron Bald Trailhead at the end of Baxter Road (off US 321, about 15.4 miles east of Gatlinburg, then just under half a mile), walk the Maddron Bald Trail about 2.9 miles (4.7 km) one way to the Albright Grove Loop, a 0.7 mile (1.1 km) loop; the NPS gives 6.5 miles (10.5 km) round trip including the loop. A short signed spur path off the loop where it starts to descend leads to the tree. Gain about 1,475 ft (450 m), moderate to steep and rough per the NPS. Limited parking at the trailhead; Wikipedia warns of car break-ins. Free to walk. Park It Forward parking tag required for any vehicle parked longer than 15 minutes: $5 a day, $15 a week, $40 a year (nps.gov/grsm/planyourvisit/fees.htm, fetched 2026-11-04); no tag on the Free Entrance Days. No park entrance fee.
trees.transport: No public transport. By car about 16 miles (26 km) east of Gatlinburg on US 321 plus half a mile on Baxter Road, roughly 30 minutes; there is no shuttle or bus to Baxter Road.
trees.verify_notes: State: Tennessee (Cocke County), not NC. Called the largest tulip tree in the national park / 'king of Albright Grove' by smokymountains.com. Measured figures: circumference 25 ft 3 in (770 cm) per appvoices 2019 (Eric Halvarson, article says it may once have stood about 135 ft; crown damaged, possibly by lightning); smokymountains.com says 'a little more than 25 feet' and 135 ft tall, dead-topped veteran. A 2014 trip report gives nearly 150 ft (not fetched, only seen in search summary). Height 41 m (135 ft) is therefore a former or estimated height, dead top. Who measured is not stated. ALIVE: no source after 2019 found that I could fetch; flagged for that reason (appvoices 2019-10-11, trip report 2016-04). A hiker review mentions many grove giants have since died; this one was not named as dead. Another giant in the grove, a snag guessed at 30 ft diameter (ilovetrees.net, April 2016) and a 15 ft diameter stump (Commons photo by Chris M Morris 2007), are dead; do not ship. PIN: OSM way 167431520 (Albright Grove Loop Trail) centre 35.7351,-83.2796 (bbox 35.7343-35.7373, -83.2808 to -83.2755). The spur sits on the descending part of the loop, which of the loop's sides is not published, so the pin marks the loop only and is approximate (within about 250 m). Hemlocks: appvoices describes an alive unnamed hemlock over 5 ft wide near mile 3 (2019); not individually locatable, not delivered. One-source US rule applies (appvoices plus smokymountains.com agree on 25 ft). NPS places page names the grove's tulip poplars and Fraser magnolias but gives no tree figures. Age not documented; sources say some trees in the grove exceed 200 years, not this one specifically. TRAIL STATUS: NPS Albright Grove page last updated 2026-01-15 carries no closure notice and a hiking club ran the route 2026-02-28 (search result only); confirm Helene damage on nps.gov/grsm alerts.

trees.name: Ramsey Cascades giant tulip poplars

location.address: Ramsey Cascades Trail, about 2.6 miles from the trailhead, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Sevier County, Tennessee (TN side)
location.neighbourhood: Greenbrier, Great Smoky Mountains National Park

trees.story:
Partway up the Ramsey Cascades Trail, three old-growth tulip poplars stand together beside the path, and the biggest, which one writer calls the king, is at least seven feet across. That diameter puts its trunk at roughly 6.7 metres round. One trail guide says several of the poplars here pass 20 feet in circumference. Nobody has published a height for any of them, or an age.

Nobody quite agrees on where they stand, either. One trail guide says mile 2.5, another 2.6, and a January 2024 account puts them nearer two miles from the trailhead. Count on about two and a half miles. The three grow in a group beside the trail.

The trail starts at the end of Ramsey Prong Road in the Greenbrier area, on the Tennessee side of the park, about five miles of mostly gravel road from US 321. It runs about 4 miles (6.4 km) to the falls, climbing 2,000 feet or more, most of it in the last two and a half miles. To the poplars and back is about 5.2 miles (8.4 km) and a moderate walk.

Floods damaged the trail in 2022 and again in summer 2024, and the latest description of the trees dates from before that second flood. The park reopened the trail full-time in 2024. Check its alerts before you drive out, and tell us if the three still stand. Parking for longer than 15 minutes needs a Park It Forward tag.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as three big tulip poplars grouped together beside the trail, the largest at least seven feet across. They stand about two and a half miles up the Ramsey Cascades Trail.
trees.access: Ramsey Cascades Trailhead at the end of Ramsey Prong Road in the Greenbrier area, about 5 miles of mostly gravel road from US 321. The trail is about 4.0 miles (6.4 km) one way, 8 miles (13 km) round trip to the falls; the giant poplars stand about 2.6 miles (4.2 km) up per trail guides (tehcc.org says mile 2.5), so about 5.2 miles (8.4 km) round trip to the trees alone. Climb about 2,000 to 2,200 ft (610 to 670 m) in total, mostly in the last 2.5 miles; strenuous to the falls, moderate to the trees. The lot is medium sized and fills on busy days. Free to walk. Park It Forward parking tag required for any vehicle parked longer than 15 minutes: $5 a day, $15 a week, $40 a year (nps.gov/grsm/planyourvisit/fees.htm, fetched 2026-11-04); no tag on the Free Entrance Days. No park entrance fee.
trees.transport: No public transport. By car about 20 minutes east of Gatlinburg to the Greenbrier entrance (NPS), then the gravel road to the trailhead. Ramsey Prong Road is partly unpaved; check current park road status before driving.
trees.verify_notes: State: Tennessee (Sevier County). The earlier lead name 'Roman Columns' appears in no fetched source and is dropped; the trees are described as 'three towering old growth tulip poplars' (tehcc.org, mile 2.5, last edited 2023-01-07), 'three large tulip poplars' at 2.6 miles (trail guide), and smliv.com (2024-01-20) says two huge yellow poplars and a third, the 'king', at least seven feet in diameter. 7 ft diameter gives girth about 670 cm (derived, pi x 213 cm); a trail guide says several poplars exceed 20 ft circumference. Mile figures conflict: smliv places them about 1.5 miles plus half a mile up; tehcc.org 2.5, other guides 2.6. Treat as an ensemble with one place to stand (the three trees are grouped beside the trail). ALIVE: smliv.com article dated 2024-01-20 describes them; tehcc.org 2023. Height not given by any source. PIN: OSM way 279159542 (Ramsey Cascades Trail, 6,147 m long, 357 vertices; the NPS and guides say about 4.0 mi, so the way is slightly short of the falls) interpolated at 2.6 mi (4,184 m) gives 35.70992,-83.31715. Mile accuracy of a trail guide is perhaps 0.2 mi, so approximate, within roughly 300 m of trail. Flagged: no NPS or measurement source for the diameter, three trail sources only. TRAIL STATUS: NPS news release says the Ramsey Cascades Trail reopened full-time in 2024 after a three-year restoration (flood damage 2022 and summer 2024 to trail and Greenbrier Road; nationalparkstraveler.org 2024-11); search found no later closure, but confirm on nps.gov/grsm alerts before a page makes access claims. Trailhead parking OSM way 227445575 at 35.7027,-83.3578.

trees.name: The Pearl Harbor Tree

location.address: Hillside above the Cades Cove Loop Road near the Native Plant Demonstration Plot, Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee (TN side)
location.neighbourhood: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park

trees.story:
When news of the attack on Pearl Harbor reached Cades Cove, Golman Myers planted a sweet gum sapling in his family's front yard. The National Park Service dates the planting to 7 December 1941, the day of the attack. One family account has the news arriving over the radio on 8 December, so the tree dates from the day of the attack or the day after. Myers died in 1945. His tree is now over 60 feet tall.

The Myers front yard is a hillside above the Cades Cove Loop Road today. A brass tribute naming veterans of the Pacific war once hung on the tree and has since been lost. In 2022 the park brought Medal of Honor recipients to visit it.

There is no sign and no official trail. Drive the one-way, 11-mile loop road to the first gravel pull-off after the Native Plant Demonstration Plot, about 3.6 miles in by one account, and take the unmarked path at the back of it, which climbs a steep hillside for a short distance. Small flags mark the tree. The loop is open to cars and bikes, but some mornings in season it is for bikes only, so check the park's schedule. Cades Cove is about an hour's drive from Gatlinburg.

The visit is free. Parking for longer than 15 minutes anywhere in the park needs a Park It Forward tag.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small flags that mark it, a sweet gum over 60 feet tall. It stands a short, steep climb up the hillside behind the first gravel pull-off after the Native Plant Demonstration Plot.
trees.access: Cades Cove Loop Road (one-way, 11 miles, open to cars and bikes; seasonal gate and Wednesday/Saturday morning bike-only periods in season, check NPS). Park at the first gravel pull-off after the Native Plant Demonstration Plot lot, about 3.6 miles into the loop by one account; an unmarked footpath at the back of the pull-off climbs a steep hillside for a short distance to the tree, which is marked with small flags. No official trail or sign. Free to visit. Park It Forward parking tag required for any vehicle parked longer than 15 minutes: $5 a day, $15 a week, $40 a year (nps.gov/grsm/planyourvisit/fees.htm, fetched 2026-11-04); no tag on the Free Entrance Days. No park entrance fee.
trees.transport: No public transport. Cades Cove is reached by car from Townsend or Gatlinburg (roughly an hour from Gatlinburg); the loop road is the only way in.
trees.verify_notes: State: Tennessee (Blount County). A sweetgum ('red gum' sapling) planted by Golman Myers, a Cades Cove resident, on 7 December 1941 after news of the Pearl Harbor attack, in what was the Myers family front yard (WVLT 2018-12-07; backwoodsadventures 2018). The family's radio story is set on 8 December in one account (WVLT); the planting date as 7 December is what the NPS release (Medal of Honor recipients visit, 2022-09-08) states. Golman died in 1945. A tag on the tree read 'Golman Myers transplanted this tree Dec. 7 1941' with 'Pearl Harbor' on the reverse (search summary only, not fetched); WVLT describes a brass tribute naming Pacific veterans, since lost. Height: over 60 ft per thesmokies.com (updated 2024-05-29), so 18 m. Girth not given. ALIVE: thesmokies.com 2024-05-29, NPS visit 2022-09-08. PIN: not a tree-level coordinate. The tree sits on the hillside above the first pull-off after the Native Plant Demonstration Plot parking lot (about 35.6057,-83.8355 per a Google Maps link in thesmokies.com); Cades Cove Missionary Baptist Church is at 35.6080,-83.8262 (Nominatim), consistent with that direction of travel. Pin is the lot; the tree is up the hill a short distance, so approximate. Age is a documented planting date for this specimen (84 to 85 years in 2025/2026). Access caveat: unmarked social path on park land; no source says it is closed or prohibited.
